title: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
source_used: TechCrunch (Equity podcast write-up, 11 Oct 2026); TechCrunch 3 Oct 2026 for Amazon's announcement
key_facts: Amazon recently followed Microsoft's lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centres.
The statement came in the middle of a longer Amazon blog post making the case that data centres are good for communities (TechCrunch, 3 Oct 2026: by AWS chief executive Matt Garman).
Microsoft made a similar announcement earlier this year.
Host Sean O'Kane says much of the backlash goes back to projects being negotiated in secret and to the industry explaining itself poorly.
Host Rebecca Bellan doubts recent moratoriums will have a lasting effect because they last only a year or two while data centres will not open for two to five years.
Host Anthony Ha says removing NDAs will not turn opponents into supporters but is a good first step; New York's moratorium is a one-year pause on permits for large projects.
The hosts discuss opinions; the article contains no new reporting on the NDA decision itself.
quote_evidence: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.
So it does seem like a good first step.
why_it_matters_hint: Secret negotiations are a main complaint of data-centre opponents, so dropping NDAs could change how projects are discussed locally, though the hosts doubt it will quickly win people over.
event_date: 2 Oct 2026 (Amazon blog post; TechCrunch report 3 Oct 2026); podcast write-up 11 Oct 2026
notes: Podcast commentary, not a news report; the news event is older than the window. The 2 Oct date and Matt Garman's name come from TechCrunch's 3 Oct 2026 article, not from the 11 Oct piece.
